topic: Pressure and pressure differences in fluids (physics only)
subject: physics

items.q: In physics, what is meant by the term 'fluid'?
items.correct: A substance that can flow: a liquid or a gas.
items.misconception: A liquid only, since a gas cannot be poured.
items.why: In everyday English 'fluid' means a runny liquid, and the word is printed on drink and medicine bottles, never on anything gaseous. In physics a fluid is anything that can flow. Gases flow, so a fluid can be either a liquid or a gas.
items.random_wrong: Anything that pours, such as dry sand.

items.q: A sealed can holds compressed air. In which direction does the air pressure exert a force on the flat top of the can?
items.correct: At right angles to the top, pushing outwards.
items.misconception: Vertically downwards, pulled by the air's weight.
items.why: Pressure is first met as an object resting on the ground, where the force really is vertically downwards. The pressure in a fluid causes a force normal to any surface, so on a vertical or sloping wall the force is not vertical.
items.random_wrong: Sideways across the top, following the airflow.

items.q: Water in a reservoir presses on a sloping side wall. How does the force from the water act on that wall?
items.correct: Normal to the wall at every point along it.
items.misconception: Vertically downwards all the way down the wall.
items.why: Pressure is first met as an object resting on the ground, where the force really is vertically downwards. The pressure in a fluid causes a force normal to any surface, so on a vertical or sloping wall the force is not vertical.
items.random_wrong: Straight downwards, in line with the water's weight.

items.q: Which equation gives the pressure at the surface of a fluid?
items.correct: pressure = (force normal to a surface)/(area of that surface)
items.misconception: pressure = (area of that surface)/(force normal to that surface)
items.why: Students remember that the equation is a division but not which quantity goes on top, so they invert it. Force is on the top of the fraction and area on the bottom: p = F/A.
items.random_wrong: pressure = (force normal to a surface) × (area of the surface)

items.q: A force of 4500 N acts at right angles to a surface of area 0.03 m². Calculate the pressure on the surface.
items.why: Dividing by a number smaller than one is rare in everyday arithmetic, so the decimal point is dropped or shifted by the wrong number of places. Check the size of the answer: dividing by a number less than 1 must make the answer larger than the number you started with.
items.random_wrong: 135 Pa

items.q: A crate presses on the floor with a force of 2400 N normal to the floor and exerts a pressure of 800 Pa. Calculate the area of contact.
items.correct: 3 m²
items.misconception: 30 m²
items.why: Dividing by a number smaller than one is rare in everyday arithmetic, so the decimal point is dropped or shifted by the wrong number of places. Check the size of the answer: dividing by a number less than 1 must make the answer larger than the number you started with.

items.q: In the equation p = F/A, what unit is the pressure p measured in?
items.correct: Pascals, written Pa.
items.misconception: Newton per metre, N/m.
items.why: Pressure and force are used as synonyms in everyday language, and the newton is the force unit students know best. Pressure is force per unit area, measured in pascals, Pa. Force alone is measured in newtons, N.
items.random_wrong: Newtons, written N.

items.q: A force of 16 N acts normal to a surface of area 200 cm². Calculate the pressure in pascals. 1 m² = 10 000 cm²
items.correct: 800 Pa
items.misconception: 8 Pa
items.why: Length conversions are done automatically by now, so students forget that area needs the conversion squared. The area in p = F/A must be in metres squared. Divide an area in cm² by 10 000.
items.random_wrong: 80 Pa

items.q: A brick of mass 2.0 kg rests flat on a bench. gravitational field strength = 9.8 N/kg  Which value is the force normal to the bench in p = F/A?
items.correct: 19.6 N, the weight of the brick.
items.misconception: 2.0 N, the mass rewritten in newtons.
items.why: Mass and weight are used interchangeably in everyday speech, and the mass is the number printed in the question. F is a force in newtons. Convert mass to weight before substituting into p = F/A.
items.random_wrong: 9.8 N, the field strength in N/kg.

items.q: A walker on soft snow puts on wide snowshoes and stops sinking in. Why?
items.correct: The larger area reduces the pressure on the snow.
items.misconception: The larger area increases the pressure on the snow.
items.why: 'More area' feels like 'more of everything', and students do not track that area is on the bottom of the fraction. Area divides the force. For a fixed normal force, doubling the area halves the pressure.
items.random_wrong: The larger area presses down harder on the snow.

items.q: Which word equation gives the pressure due to a column of liquid?
items.correct: pressure = height of the column × density of the liquid × gravitational field strength
items.misconception: pressure = width of the column × density of the liquid × gravitational field strength
items.why: More liquid feels like more pressure, so students bring in the width or area of the container. p = h ρ g contains no area term. A wide tank and a narrow tube filled to the same height give the same pressure at the base.
items.random_wrong: pressure = height of the column × area of the column × gravitational field strength

items.q: In the equation p = h ρ g, how is the height h of the liquid column found from the other quantities?
items.correct: Divide the pressure by ρ g.
items.misconception: Multiply the pressure by ρ g.
items.why: Rearranging is done by pattern-matching rather than by inverting the operation. ρ and g multiply h, so to undo them you divide the pressure by ρ g.
items.random_wrong: Divide ρ g by the pressure value.

items.q: In the equation p = h ρ g, which units must be used for p and for h?
items.correct: p in pascals, Pa and h in metres, m
items.misconception: p in pascals, Pa and h in centimetres, cm
items.why: Density is often measured in g/cm³ in practical work, so that unit feels equally valid. The equation as given in the specification requires density in kg/m³.
items.random_wrong: p in newtons, N and h in centimetres, cm

items.q: In the equation p = h ρ g, what unit must the density ρ be given in?
items.correct: Kilograms per metre cubed, kg/m³.
items.misconception: Kilograms per litre, kg/l.
items.why: Density is often measured in g/cm³ in practical work, so that unit feels equally valid. The equation as given in the specification requires density in kg/m³.
items.random_wrong: Grams per centimetre cubed, g/cm³.

items.q: An exam question asks for the pressure at the bottom of a column of sea water. What does the specification say about the gravitational field strength g?
items.correct: Its value will be given in the question, in N/kg.
items.misconception: It must be recalled from memory as 9.8 N/kg.
items.why: Rounded values are used in early lessons and become fixed in memory. The specification states that the value of g will be given in any calculation, so read it from the question.
items.random_wrong: It is measured in newtons, N, and is recalled.

items.q: Explain why the pressure at a point in a liquid increases as that point gets deeper.
items.correct: A taller column of liquid lies above it, weighing more.
items.misconception: The liquid becomes denser lower down, where it is squashed.
items.why: Students transfer the idea of compression from gases, where density really does change, to liquids. The density of a liquid is effectively constant. It is the greater height of liquid above the point that raises the pressure.
items.random_wrong: The liquid flows downwards, pressing harder low down.

items.q: Two tanks are filled to the same depth, one with water and one with mercury. Why is the pressure at the base greater in the mercury?
items.correct: Mercury is denser, so the column above weighs more.
items.misconception: The mercury must be filled to a greater depth.
items.why: Depth is the variable students meet first and can feel in a swimming pool, so it crowds out density. Pressure is h × ρ × g. A denser liquid gives a heavier column above the point and so a greater pressure.
items.random_wrong: Mercury is denser, so its column is taller than water.

items.q: Calculate the pressure due to a column of water of height 25 m. density of water = 1000 kg/m³  gravitational field strength = 9.8 N/kg
items.why: Rearranging is done by pattern-matching rather than by inverting the operation. ρ and g multiply h, so to undo them you divide the pressure by ρ g.

items.q: A diver swims from a depth of 8.0 m to a depth of 12.0 m. density of sea water = 1030 kg/m³  gravitational field strength = 9.8 N/kg  Calculate the increase in pressure on the diver.
items.why: The question mentions two depths, and students grab the one that seems to be 'the answer depth'. A difference in pressure comes from a difference in height, so substitute the change in depth.

items.q: A sealed can is held completely under water. Why does the water exert a resultant upward force on it?
items.correct: Pressure on its bottom face exceeds that on its top.
items.misconception: Water pushes up on the bottom and not down on the top.
items.why: Only the upward result is remembered, so students drop the downward push that is being outweighed. There is a force on both surfaces. The bottom is deeper, so the pressure there is greater and the resultant force is upwards.
items.random_wrong: The can is full of air, which is lighter than the water.

items.q: A submerged object experiences a greater pressure on its bottom surface than on its top surface. What is the resultant upward force called?
items.correct: The upthrust on the object.
items.misconception: The force by which upthrust beats weight.
items.why: 'Floating up' is read as an unbalanced upward force rather than as equilibrium. A floating object is in equilibrium, so the upthrust equals the weight. A larger upthrust would accelerate it upwards.
items.random_wrong: A normal contact force from the water below.

items.q: A solid block is lowered into a tank of water and floats. Which statement explains why it floats?
items.correct: Its density is lower than the density of the water.
items.misconception: It is lighter than water, whatever its size or shape.
items.why: Everyday examples compare a stone with a cork without controlling for volume. Floating depends on density, not weight alone. A heavy object with a large volume can have a low density and float.
items.random_wrong: The upthrust on it is larger than its own weight.

items.q: Which statement best describes a simple model of the Earth's atmosphere?
items.correct: A thin layer of air round the Earth that thins with altitude.
items.misconception: A deep layer of gas that gets denser as altitude rises.
items.why: Air is invisible and feels identical everywhere a student has ever been. The atmosphere gets less dense with increasing altitude, which is why there is less air above a high surface.
items.random_wrong: A thick layer of air of the same density at all heights.

items.q: Explain why atmospheric pressure at the top of a mountain is lower than at sea level.
items.correct: There is less air above, so fewer molecules collide.
items.misconception: Gravity is much weaker at the top of a high mountain.
items.why: Height is associated with escaping gravity, as in pictures of astronauts floating. Gravity is almost unchanged over a few kilometres. What changes is the amount of air above the surface.
items.random_wrong: The air up there is colder, so it presses down less hard.

items.q: Is sand a fluid?
items.correct: No. Sand is a solid made of grains; a fluid is a liquid or a gas.
items.misconception: Anything that can be poured is a fluid, so dry sand and sugar count as fluids.
items.why: Pouring is the visible test students apply, and powders pour just as liquids do. The specification defines a fluid as a liquid or a gas. Powders are solids, however easily they pour.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A liquid presses on a sloping wall. Which way does the force act?
items.correct: At right angles to the sloping wall at every point on it.
items.misconception: The force acts along the surface, in the direction the fluid is flowing.
items.why: Students picture water sliding down a wall and assume the push follows the flow. Pressure produces a force normal to the surface. Flow direction does not set the direction of that force.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How big is the atmosphere compared with the Earth?
items.correct: It is a thin layer of air relative to the size of the Earth.
items.misconception: The atmosphere is a huge, deep blanket, far thicker than the Earth is wide.
items.why: Diagrams exaggerate the atmosphere so it can be seen, and space feels limitless. The atmosphere is thin compared with the size of the Earth, and it fades out with altitude.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What causes atmospheric pressure at a surface?
items.correct: Air molecules colliding with the surface.
items.misconception: It is the wind: moving air blowing against a surface is what presses on it.
items.why: Wind is the only time students feel air pushing on them. Still air exerts pressure too, because its molecules are always colliding with the surface.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Why is the pressure lower at the top of a mountain?
items.correct: Less air lies above, so the weight of air above the surface is smaller.
items.misconception: The air up there is colder, and cold air presses less hard on a surface.
items.why: Cold is the most obvious difference at altitude, so it is offered as the cause of everything. The change in pressure comes from the reduced amount of air above the surface, not from its temperature.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

specSource: AQA GCSE Physics (8463) specification; section 4.5.5 Pressure and pressure differences in fluids (physics only)
